newsitem.title: USA: American confident it will win Miami rate dispute.
newsitem.headline: American confident it will win Miami rate dispute.

text.p: American Airlines said Tuesday it is confident the U.S. Department of Transporation will uphold the rate plan that Florida's Dade County set for the carrier's new bond-financed terminal at Miami International Airport.

"We believe that this issue will receive a full and fair hearing before the DOT itself and that ultimately Dade County and American will prevail in this issue," said Al Becker, a spokesman for the airline, a unit of AMR Corp.

American and the county, which runs the airport, were dealt a setback Tuesday when an administrative law judge in Washington issued an opinion that the fee schedule that will finance the new construction was "unfair and unreasonable."

Six other airlines sued Dade County in U.S. District Court last year, alleging that the funding formula, which is pro-rated according to the number of flights each carrier operates, would unfairly force them to help pay for a terminal that only American could use.
They sought to bar the county from issuing revenue bonds for the project, complaining that the American terminal was an overly lavish "Taj Mahal" compared to the facilities they use.
The American terminal is part of a 10-year, $3.6 billion expansion plan that also calls for a new terminal for the other carriers, plus a new runway and added cargo space.

In a 101-page decision Tuesday, Washington, D.C. Administrative Law Judge Ronnie Yoder agreed that the new American terminal was "incomparable to the facilities provided or to be provided to the joint carriers."
Since only American will use the new terminal, the judge found the fees resulted in "discriminatory treatment of the other carriers."
The Department of Transportation must review the findings and make a final decision by March 19.
"Obviously we are disappointed by Mr Yoder's opinion and we obviously do not concur," Becker said.

Dade County aviation officials could not be reached for comment. But Becker said the pro-rated fee structure had long been used at Miami International and that American had often helped pay for facilities there it does not use.

"The equalization system at MIA was apporoved by all the carriers back in 1990 and no airlines at the airport raised any objection to this methodology until this part of the project (the American terminal) was developed," Becker said.
Additionally, he said, the Pittsburgh and San Francisco airports, where some of the plaintiff carriers have major hubs, use the same fee structure.
American operates 52 percent of the flights out of Miami International, which it uses as a major hub for Latin America and the Caribbean.
The six plaintiff airlines are Air Canada, Delta Air Lines, Trans World Airlines Inc, USAir Group Inc, United Airlines, a unit of UAL Corp and Lufthansa.
The Florida judge who initially heard the suit decided she did not have jurisdiction over fees and referred that part of the suit to the U.S. Department of Transportation.
